podcast.body: On the week ending August 4, 1984, this song was in its fifth and final week at number one on the Hot 100. It went on to be named Billboard's top hit of the year, a rare instance where a year's biggest hit was also considered its best. "When princes when Doves Cry was in its fifth and final week at number one on the hot 100. On its way to being named billboards top hit of the year."

podcast.body: This lead-off single from the "Purple Rain" album is a rare example of a mass-appeal pop song that is also "bleeding-edge art." Prince famously removed the bass line, finding it sounded better without it. The song spent five weeks at number one and featured striking curious poses, baroque imagery, a chorus that sounded like family therapy, searing guitars, and pinging Linn drum machines. It "broke all the rules" musically but succeeded by Billboard's criteria of longevity, timing, radio ubiquity, massive sales, and cultural omnipresence, commanding a year packed with totemic hits. "A song with everything except a bass line, Prince removed it and realized it sounded better that way."

podcast.body: This song was the winner of the 1984 Billboard Song of the Summer and is recognized as Prince's biggest hit, notably achieved by "taking the bass line out," a contrast to Sting's success the prior year. It served as the lead single to his "Summary Cinematic Magnum Opus Purple Rain" and was a top hit of one of Pop's greatest years. The lyrics explicitly mention "sweat," solidifying its status as a "hot weather anthem." "Prince even sings about sweat right in the lyrics, so you know it's a hot weather anthem."
